recipe.history:
Roquefort is one of the world's oldest and most revered blue cheeses, originating in the limestone caves of Combalou near the village of Roquefort-sur-Soulzon in the Aveyron region of southern France. According to legend, a young shepherd left his lunch of bread and ewe's milk cheese in one of the region's cool, natural caves while he pursued a beautiful girl, and when he returned weeks later he found his cheese transformed — veined with blue-green mold and alive with a sharp, complex flavor unlike anything he had tasted before. Whether myth or truth, the reality of Roquefort's origins stretches back well over a thousand years: Charlemagne reportedly tasted it in 769 AD and was so enchanted that he ordered two cartloads sent to his court annually. In 1411, King Charles VI of France granted the villagers of Roquefort a monopoly on the ripening of the cheese, making it one of the first foodstuffs in history to receive legal protection of its origin. Today, Roquefort carries an AOC (Appellation d'Origine Contrôlée) designation, meaning it can only be produced from the raw milk of Lacaune ewes and aged in those same ancient caves, where the natural Penicillium roqueforti mold gives the cheese its unmistakable ivory interior threaded with bold blue-green veins, a crumbly but creamy texture, and a flavor that is simultaneously buttery, tangy, salty, and fierce.

Roquefort's journey into the American burger canon is a story of immigration, ambition, and the relentless democratization of fine ingredients. French immigrants and chefs began introducing pungent blue cheeses to upscale American dining rooms in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, where Roquefort dressing — a thick, creamy blend of the crumbled cheese with buttermilk or sour cream — became a staple of steakhouse salad bars from New York to Kansas City. As American food culture evolved through the mid-twentieth century and the hamburger rose from roadside novelty to cultural icon, creative cooks began raiding the cheese cart and dropping wedges of Roquefort directly onto beef patties sizzling on flat-top grills. The fat in the cheese melted into the crust of the patty, cutting through the beef's richness with its salt and funk in a way that milder cheeses simply could not. By the 1980s and 1990s, the Roquefort burger had become a fixture on bistro and gastropub menus across the country — a signal to diners that the kitchen took its craft seriously. Paired with sweet caramelized onions or sharp watercress to balance the cheese's intensity, it represents one of the most successful transatlantic collaborations in culinary history.

I remember the first time I had a Roquefort burger — not in a restaurant, but at my uncle's backyard in Plymouth, Massachusetts, on an overcast August afternoon when the smell of salt air drifted in off the harbor. He had driven to a specialty cheese shop that morning and come back cradling a wrapped wedge like it was something precious, because to him it was. He crumbled it over patties on a charcoal kettle grill, and the cheese hissed and softened and sent up a smell that was equal parts funky and magnificent. We ate standing up at a wooden picnic table, no plates, just paper towels, and no one said much because we were all too busy eating. The sky was the color of old pewter and the grass needed cutting and everything was exactly right. That burger tasted like a secret — like something you weren't supposed to be able to get in a backyard in a small New England town — and every Plymouth Roquefort Burger I've made since has been an attempt to return to that afternoon, to that particular quality of light and salt and smoke.

There is only one correct internal temperature for a beef burger, and it is medium rare: 130–135°F (54–57°C), with a warm, pink, yielding center and a deeply seared, caramelous crust. To cook a burger beyond this point is to make a series of irreversible mistakes. Above 140°F the myosin proteins in the beef tighten aggressively, squeezing out the intramuscular fat and juices that carry flavor, and by the time you reach the gray, crumbling well-done territory north of 160°F you are no longer eating a burger so much as a puck of compressed regret. Medium rare is not recklessness — it is respect for the animal, for the grind, and for everyone sitting down at the table. It is the temperature at which fat and collagen are just beginning to melt but the cell structure still holds enough moisture to flood the palate on the first bite. Use fresh, high-quality beef from a trusted butcher, handle it gently, season it at the last moment, and pull it from the heat at 130°F. Tent it briefly and let carryover do the rest. The reward is a burger that is tender and juicy and genuinely tasting of beef — a canvas worthy of a cheese as extraordinary as Roquefort.
ingredients: 300g (2 1/3 cups) bread flour, plus extra for dusting
3 large eggs, room temperature (2 for dough, 1 for egg wash)
85g (6 tbsp) unsalted butter, softened and cubed
680g (1.5 lbs) beef chuck, 80/20 fat ratio, freshly ground or coarsely ground by butcher
1 tbsp neutral oil (such as grapeseed or canola), for the pan or grill
115g (4 oz) Roquefort cheese, crumbled, divided (half for sauce, half for topping)
2 large yellow onions, thinly sliced into half-moons
60ml (1/4 cup) dry white wine or dry vermouth
2 cups fresh watercress or arugula, thick stems removed
Softened unsalted butter, for toasting buns
instructions: 1. MAKE THE BRIOCHE BUN DOUGH: In the bowl of a stand mixer fitted with the dough hook, combine warm milk, sugar, and yeast. Stir gently and let sit 5–10 minutes until foamy and fragrant. Add 2 eggs and mix on low to combine.

2. Add bread flour and salt to the yeast mixture. Mix on low speed until a shaggy dough forms, about 2 minutes. Increase to medium speed and knead for 5 minutes until the dough starts to come together and pull away from the sides of the bowl.

3. With the mixer running on medium-low, add the softened butter one cube at a time, waiting until each piece is fully incorporated before adding the next — this will take about 8–10 minutes total. Once all butter is added, increase to medium-high and knead for a further 5 minutes until the dough is smooth, supple, and passes the windowpane test (a small piece stretched thin should become nearly translucent without tearing).

4. Shape the dough into a ball, place it in a lightly oiled bowl, cover tightly with plastic wrap, and refrigerate for at least 8 hours or overnight. Cold fermentation develops flavor and makes the enriched dough much easier to shape.

5. SHAPE AND PROOF THE BUNS: Remove dough from the refrigerator. Divide into 4 equal portions (approximately 145g each). Working one at a time on an unfloured surface, cup your hand over the dough and use a circular rolling motion to create surface tension, forming tight, smooth rounds. Place on a parchment-lined baking sheet at least 3 inches apart. Cover loosely with plastic wrap and let proof at room temperature for 2–3 hours until visibly puffed and pillowy.

6. Preheat oven to 375°F (190°C). Beat the remaining egg with 1 tbsp water to make egg wash. Gently brush the tops of the proofed buns with egg wash and sprinkle with flaky sea salt. Bake for 16–20 minutes, rotating the pan once at the halfway mark, until deep golden brown and the internal temperature reads 190°F (88°C). Transfer to a wire rack and cool completely before slicing.

7. CARAMELIZE THE ONIONS: In a wide, heavy-bottomed skillet (preferably cast iron or stainless), melt butter with olive oil over medium heat. Add the sliced onions and salt. Stir to coat, then spread into an even layer. Cook over medium-low to low heat, stirring every 5–7 minutes, for 45–60 minutes total. The onions should slowly turn from translucent to pale gold to a rich amber-brown. If they are browning too fast or sticking, reduce heat and add a splash of water. When deeply caramelized, add the thyme leaves and white wine, scraping up any fond from the bottom of the pan. Cook another 2–3 minutes until the wine has evaporated. Remove from heat and set aside.

8. COOK THE BACON: Lay bacon slices in a cold cast iron skillet, then set over medium heat. Cook, turning occasionally, until fat is rendered and bacon is crispy and browned, about 8–10 minutes. Transfer to a paper-towel-lined plate and set aside.

9. MAKE THE ROQUEFORT CREAM SAUCE: In a medium bowl, combine half the crumbled Roquefort (about 55g / 2 oz) with the sour cream, mayonnaise, lemon juice, Worcestershire sauce, white wine vinegar, and black pepper. Use a fork to mash and stir vigorously until mostly smooth with some small crumbles remaining for texture. Taste and adjust seasoning — Roquefort is very salty, so additional salt is unlikely to be needed. Cover and refrigerate until ready to use.

10. FORM THE PATTIES: Remove ground beef from the refrigerator 20 minutes before cooking to take the chill off. Gently divide into 4 equal portions (about 170g / 6 oz each). Handle the beef as little as possible — overworking compacts the proteins and produces a dense, tough patty. Loosely form each portion into a round, flat disc approximately 4 inches in diameter and 3/4-inch thick. Use your thumb to press a shallow dimple in the center of each patty (this prevents the center from doming during cooking). Do NOT season with salt until immediately before cooking, as premature salting draws out moisture and begins to denature the proteins.

11. COOK THE PATTIES TO MEDIUM RARE: Heat a cast iron skillet or heavy griddle over high heat until smoking hot, about 3–4 minutes. Add the neutral oil and swirl to coat. Season the patties generously on both sides with kosher salt and cracked black pepper immediately before placing them in the pan. Lay patties down away from you and do not touch them for 2.5–3 minutes. You want a deep, dark mahogany crust to form — do not press down on the patties at any point. Flip once and cook for a further 2–2.5 minutes on the second side.

12. APPLY ROQUEFORT AND CHECK TEMPERATURE: In the last 60 seconds of cooking, divide the remaining crumbled Roquefort (55g / 2 oz) evenly over the tops of the four patties. If working on a grill, close the lid briefly to help the cheese soften. Remove patties from heat when an instant-read thermometer inserted into the thickest part reads 130–132°F (54–56°C). Transfer to a warm plate, tent loosely with foil, and rest for 3–4 minutes — carryover cooking will bring them to 133–135°F (56–57°C), the perfect medium-rare. Do not skip the rest: it allows the juices to redistribute throughout the patty.

13. TOAST THE BUNS: While the patties rest, slice each brioche bun in half horizontally. Butter the cut sides lightly with softened butter. Toast in a dry skillet over medium heat, cut-side down, for 60–90 seconds until golden and lightly crisped. Remove from heat.

14. ASSEMBLE THE BURGER: Spread a generous spoonful of Roquefort cream sauce on both the cut top and bottom bun. On the bottom bun, layer watercress or arugula, then a slice or two of heirloom tomato. Place the rested patty (topped with its melted Roquefort crumbles) on top of the tomato. Add a slice or two of crispy bacon, then a heap of caramelized onions. Cap with the top bun, pressing down gently. Serve immediately.
